beats.say: How many 2 digit numbers are odd? Let's count them without writing every single one.
The 2 digit numbers start at 10 and stop at 99.
What makes a number odd?

choices: it has an odd number of digits
ask.ifNot: Look at 11 and 12 on the board. 12 ends in 2, so it is even. 11 ends in 1, so it is odd. Only the last digit decides.

beats.say: Take the numbers that start with 1. The odd ones are 11, 13, 15, 17 and 19. That is 5 of them.
The twenties give 5 more: 21, 23, 25, 27 and 29. In fact, every tens digit gives exactly 5 odd numbers.
So how many different tens digits can a 2 digit number have?

ask.ifNot: The tens digit can be 1, 2, 3 and so on up to 9. It cannot be 0, because then the number would have only 1 digit.

beats.say: 9 tens digits, with 5 odd numbers for each. 9 times 5 is 45.
Check it another way. From 10 to 99 there are 90 numbers, and odd and even take turns. Half of 90 is 45.
So to count without listing, find how many choices there are for each digit, then multiply.
How many 3 digit numbers are odd? There are far too many to list, so we need a clever count.
The 3 digit numbers run from 100 up to 999. How many numbers is that?

ask.ifNot: Count every number from 1 to 999, and there are 999. Now take away the 99 short ones, 1 to 99, and what is left is the 3 digit numbers.

beats.say: 999 minus 99 is 900. So there are 900 numbers with 3 digits.
Now look at how they go: 100 is even, 101 is odd, 102 is even. Odd and even take turns, all the way to 999.
So what part of those 900 numbers is odd?

ask.ifNot: Odd and even take turns, one after the other. The list starts on an even number and ends on an odd one, so they share it equally.

beats.say: Half of 900 is 450. There are 450 odd numbers with 3 digits.
Check by choosing digits. 9 choices for the hundreds, 10 for the tens, and 5 odd digits for the ones. 9 times 10 times 5 is 450 again.
Careful not to stop at 900: that is all the 3 digit numbers, odd and even together. Count the whole list, then take half.
We have the digits 3, 4 and 5, and each may be used once. How many different 3 digit numbers can we build?
A 3 digit number has 3 places to fill: hundreds, tens and ones. Let's fill them one at a time.
How many digits can we choose from for the hundreds place?

ask.ifNot: Any of our digits can go first: the 3, the 4 or the 5. That makes 3 choices.

beats.say: Suppose the 3 goes first. Each digit is used only once, so only the 4 and the 5 are left for the tens. That is 2 choices.
And once the tens place is filled, just 1 digit is left for the ones.
So how do we get the total?

ask.ifNot: Each first digit can be followed by 2 different tens digits, and then by 1 ones digit. Choices that follow one another are multiplied.

beats.say: 3 times 2 times 1 is 6. We can build 6 numbers.
Let's list them to be sure. 345, 354, 435, 453, 534, 543. Yes, 6 numbers.
Careful: 9 would be right only if a digit could be used again. Used once, the choices shrink each time: 3, then 2, then 1.
The bill is 156.50 rupees. Rohan, Aarav and Meera pay part of it, and Kiran and Priya share the rest equally. How much does each of those two pay?

board.text: The rest is shared equally by 2

beats.say: What do we find first?

ask.ifNot: Kiran and Priya share only what is left of the bill. To know what is left, we first need the total the other 3 have paid.

beats.say: Add Meera's 29.85, and the three of them have paid 114.20.
Take that from the bill. 156.50 minus 114.20 leaves 42.30.
Careful: 42.30 is for Kiran and Priya together. It is one of the choices, but the question asks what each of them pays.
Half of 42 is 21, and half of 0.30 is 0.15. So each of them pays 21.15 rupees.
Check by adding up all 5 payments. 114.20, plus 21.15, plus 21.15, makes 156.50, the whole bill.
So: add what has been paid, subtract to find what is left, and then share it. Three small steps, in that order.
Priya buys 4.75 kilograms of kaju katli and 3.25 kilograms of rasgulla, and packs all of it equally into 8 gift boxes. What is the weight of sweets in each box?

board.text: 4.75 kg and 3.25 kg of sweets, in 8 equal boxes

beats.say: The story also gives two prices, 560.80 and 184.40 rupees. Do we need them?

choices: No: we only need the weights
ask.ifNot: Read the last line again. It asks for the weight in each box. Prices tell us about money, and nobody asked about money.

beats.say: So leave the prices alone. That is the trap in this question: extra numbers that are just passing by.
All the sweets together: 4.75 plus 3.25. Look at the parts after the point. 0.75 and 0.25 make exactly 1 whole.
So 4 plus 3, plus 1 more, is 8 kilograms of sweets.
8 kilograms shared equally into 8 boxes. 8 divided by 8 is 1. Each box holds 1 kilogram.
Check: 8 boxes of 1 kilogram make 8 kilograms, which is all the sweets.
Before you calculate, ask what the question wants. Then use only the numbers that help.
Ravi and Priya sell laddoos for 2 days, put all their money together, and split it equally. How much does each get?
Each seller keeps the same price on both days. So first add up how many each one sold. Ravi: 24 and 16 make 40. Priya: 36 and 28 make 64.
Ravi's money is 40 times 12.75. Now 4 times 12.75 is 51, so 40 times is 10 times as much: 510 rupees.
Priya's money is 64 times 9.50. 64 nines are 576, and 64 halves are 32. Together, 608 rupees.
They put the money together and split it equally. So what do we do with 510 and 608?

ask.ifNot: Putting money together means adding. And splitting it equally between 2 people means halving the total.

beats.say: Half of 1118 is 559. Each person gets 559 rupees.
Check: 2 shares of 559 make 1118, all the money.
Careful: Ravi earned 510 himself, and that is one of the choices. But the money was pooled first. Find each total, add, then share.
Riya starts with 100 rupees. She buys tea leaves, sugar and milk, and then she finds a 2 rupee coin. How much does she have now?
What should we work out first?

choices: the price of just one thing
the money she has at the end
ask.ifNot: Several prices went out of the purse. Add them into one total first, and then there is only one subtraction to do.

beats.say: Line up the decimal points and add. 32.45 plus 18.70 is 51.15.
Then 51.15 plus 25.50 is 76.65. That is everything Riya spent.
Now take that away from the 100 rupees. Write 100 with a point and two zeros, so the paise have something to be taken from. 100 minus 76.65 leaves 23.35.
Is 23.35 rupees the answer?

choices: No: add the 2 rupees she found
ask.ifNot: Read the end of the story again. Riya picked up a 2 rupee coin on her way back. That is money coming in, so it is added on.

beats.say: 23.35 plus 2 is 25.35. Riya now has 25.35 rupees.
Check by going backwards. 25.35 minus the 2 found is 23.35, and 23.35 plus the 76.65 spent is 100, the money at the start.
So in a money story: add up what went out, subtract it once, then add what came in. And keep the decimal points in line.
Arjun's performance score is his 5 numbers added up and divided by 5. The qualifying score is 0.8 of 20. How far apart are the two scores?
Two scores to find, and then we compare them. Start with Arjun's. Look for friendly pairs: 15.75 and 16.25 make 32, because 0.75 and 0.25 make 1.
And 12.5 with 17.5 makes 30, because the two halves make 1.
32 plus 30 plus the 18 is 80.
80 divided by 5 is 16. That is Arjun's performance score.
Now the qualifying score: 0.8 of 20. What does the word of tell us to do?

ask.ifNot: In maths, of means multiply. 0.8 of 20 is 8 tenths of 20, and that is 0.8 times 20.

beats.say: One tenth of 20 is 2. So 8 tenths of 20 is 8 times 2, which is 16.
Both scores are 16! So the gap between them is 16 minus 16, which is 0.
Check the first score: 5 scores of 16 would total 80, and that is exactly what Arjun's 5 numbers added up to.
Don't be put off by an answer of 0. It means Arjun has exactly the score he needs. Find each amount on its own, then compare.
Ravi's father sells chai in 3 sizes, and pays for milk, tea leaves and sugar. We want his profit from the match.
Careful, some numbers here are just passing by. 150, 250 and 400 millilitres tell us how big the cups are. They do nothing to the money.
What is profit?

ask.ifNot: Profit is what you really gain. Count the money that came in, then take away what had to be paid out.

beats.say: Start with the money earned. Small cups: 24 at 12.50 each. 24 times 12 is 288, and 24 halves are 12 more. That is 300 rupees.
Medium cups: 36 times 18 is 648, and 36 times 0.75 is 27. Together, 675 rupees.
Large cups: 20 times 28 is 560, and 20 times 0.25 is 5. Together, 565 rupees.
Add the three: 300 plus 675 plus 565 is 1540 rupees earned.
Now the spending: 485.60 on milk, 132.40 on tea leaves and 97.50 on sugar. Together that is 715.50.
Profit is earned minus spent. 1540 minus 715.50 is 824.50 rupees.
Check: profit plus spending should give back the earnings. 824.50 plus 715.50 is 1540.
So for profit: add up everything earned, add up everything spent, and subtract. And leave out the numbers that are not about money.
Ravi spent his Diwali money on 3 things and still has 200.50 rupees left. His sister Priya was given 150 rupees less than Ravi. How much was Priya given?
Before we can find Priya's money, what must we know?

ask.ifNot: Priya's amount is measured from what Ravi was given, right at the start. So that starting amount is the first thing to find.

beats.say: Ravi's gift went two ways: some was spent, and some is still with him. Put the two back together, and we have the whole gift.
Add the spending, with the decimal points in line. 247.50 plus 183.75 is 431.25.
Add the third, 118.25, and he spent 549.50 in all.
Now add what he has left. 549.50 plus 200.50 is 750. So Ravi was given 750 rupees.
Careful: 750 is Ravi's money, and it is one of the choices. But the question asks about Priya.
Priya was given 150 less. 750 minus 150 is 600 rupees.
Check: 600 plus 150 is 750, Ravi's gift. And 750 minus the 549.50 he spent leaves 200.50. It all fits.
When a story tells you what was spent and what is left, add them to get back to the start. Then answer the question that was asked.
Kavya pours 5.4 litres of mango lassi equally into 12 glasses. How much goes into each glass?
There are more glasses than litres. So each glass gets less than 1 litre. Keep that in mind for later.
Dividing is easier in smaller pieces. 5.4 is the same as 5.40, and 5.40 is 540 hundredths.
Now share 540 among 12. Split 540 into 480 and 60. 480 divided by 12 is 40, and 60 divided by 12 is 5. So that is 45.
45 what? How many litres is in each glass?

ask.ifNot: We shared out hundredths, so each glass has 45 hundredths. And remember, each glass must get less than 1 litre.

beats.say: 45 hundredths is written 0.45. Each glass gets 0.45 litres.
Check by multiplying back. 12 times 45 is 540, so 12 times 0.45 is 5.40. That is our 5.4 litres.
To divide a decimal, turn it into tenths or hundredths, divide as whole numbers, then turn back. And always ask: should the answer be more than 1, or less?
Rohan ran the race in 14.38 seconds. Kiran was 1.65 seconds faster. What was Kiran's time?
Kiran was faster. So is his time more than Rohan's, or less?

choices: more: faster means a bigger number
ask.ifNot: In a race, the faster runner finishes sooner. Sooner means fewer seconds on the clock. So Kiran's time is smaller.

beats.say: So we subtract: 14.38 minus 1.65, with the decimal points in line.
Start on the right, with the hundredths. 8 minus 5 is 3.
Tenths: 3 minus 6 cannot be done. So borrow 1 from the 4 ones. The 4 becomes 3, and we have 13 tenths. 13 minus 6 is 7.
Ones: careful, the 4 is now a 3. 3 minus 1 is 2. And the 1 ten comes straight down.
So Kiran's time is 12.73 seconds.
Check by adding back. 12.73 plus 1.65 should be Rohan's time, and it is 14.38.
Two things to remember. Faster means less time, so subtract. And after a borrow, the column next door has changed.
Riya has 500 rupees. She buys 3 boxes of sparklers, 4 packets of diyas, and a bag to carry them. How much does she have left?
Three kinds of spending. What is the plan?

choices: cost each kind, add, take from 500
ask.ifNot: The prices say each. So 45.75 is for one box, and 32.50 is for one packet. We must multiply by how many she buys before we add.

beats.say: Sparklers: 3 times 45 is 135, and 3 times 0.75 is 2.25. So 137.25 rupees.
Diyas: 4 times 32 is 128, and 4 halves are 2 more. So 130 rupees.
Now add everything. 137.25 plus 130 is 267.25.
Don't leave the bag behind. It is only one small thing, so it is easy to forget. 267.25 plus 12.25 is 279.50.
Riya had 500. 500 minus 279.50 is 220.50 rupees left.
Check: what she spent and what she has left should make 500. 279.50 plus 220.50 is 500.
So: multiply for each kind, add up every single thing, and subtract once from the money she started with.
Ravi spent his Diwali money on 3 things and still has 124.50 rupees left. His sister Priya was given 350 rupees less than Ravi. How much was Priya given?
The story never says how much Ravi was given. Which amount do we need first?

ask.ifNot: Priya's amount is measured from what Ravi was given, right at the start. So that starting amount is the first thing to find.

beats.say: Ravi's gift went two ways: some was spent, and some is still with him. Put the two back together, and we have the whole gift.
Add the spending, with the decimal points in line. 247.50 plus 183.75 is 431.25.
Add the third, 94.25, and he spent 525.50 in all.
Now add what he has left. 525.50 plus 124.50 is 650. So Ravi was given 650 rupees.
Careful: 650 is Ravi's money, and it is one of the choices. But the question asks about Priya.
Priya was given 350 less. 650 minus 350 is 300 rupees.
Check: 300 plus 350 is 650, Ravi's gift. And 650 minus the 525.50 he spent leaves 124.50. It all fits.
Money spent plus money left takes you back to the start. And always check whose money the question wants.
Priya has 2.5 litres of mango pulp, and each glass of lassi needs 0.375 litres. She makes as many full glasses as she can. How much pulp is left over?

board.text: 2.5 litres of pulp, 0.375 litres for each glass
Left over after the full glasses = ?

beats.say: Let's count up in glasses. 2 glasses use 0.75 litres, and 4 glasses use 1.5 litres.
6 glasses use 2.25 litres. That is still inside our 2.5 litres.
Can she make a 7th full glass?

choices: Yes: there is still some pulp left
ask.ifNot: There is some pulp left, but is it enough? 7 glasses would need 2.625 litres, and that is more than the 2.5 she has.

beats.say: So 6 full glasses it is, using 2.25 litres.
Now the left over. Write 2.5 as 2.50, so the points line up. 2.50 minus 2.25 is 0.25 litres.
Does that make sense? 0.25 is less than 0.375, so it really is too little for another glass.
Careful: a full glass cannot be part of a glass. Count the full glasses, find what they use, and subtract that from the start.
Aarav has 100 rupees of gift money. He buys a toy flute and a box of sweets, and then finds 5.25 rupees in his jacket pocket. How much does he have now?
What should we work out first?

choices: the price of just one thing
the money he has at the end
ask.ifNot: Several prices went out of the purse. Add them into one total first, and then there is only one subtraction to do.

beats.say: Line up the decimal points and add. 23.45 plus 31.80 is 55.25. That is everything Aarav spent.
Now take that away from the 100 rupees. Write 100 with a point and two zeros, so the paise have something to be taken from. 100 minus 55.25 leaves 44.75.
Is 44.75 rupees the answer?

choices: No: add the 5.25 rupees he found
ask.ifNot: Read the end of the story again. Aarav found 5.25 rupees in his pocket and added it to his money. That is money coming in, so it is added on.

beats.say: 44.75 plus 5.25 is 50. Aarav now has 50 rupees.
Check by going backwards. 50 minus the 5.25 found is 44.75, and 44.75 plus the 55.25 spent is 100, the money at the start.
Spend, so subtract. Find, so add. And a neat round answer like this one is a good sign that the decimals were lined up properly.
Ananya has 3 strips of lights, each 2.75 metres long. She cuts 0.6 metres off, and shares what is left equally among 4 sections. How long is each section's share?

board.text: 3 strips of 2.75 m. Cut off 0.6 m. Share by 4.

beats.say: Three steps, in the order the story tells them: multiply, subtract, divide.
3 strips of 2.75 metres. 3 times 2 is 6, and 3 times 0.75 is 2.25. So 8.25 metres in all.
Now cut off 0.6 metres. How should we write 0.6, to subtract it from 8.25?

ask.ifNot: 0.6 is 6 tenths. A zero on the end changes nothing, but it puts the 6 under the tenths of 8.25, where it belongs.

beats.say: 8.25 minus 0.60 is 7.65 metres.
Now share 7.65 among 4 sections. Halve it, then halve again. Half of 7.65 is 3.825.
And half of 3.825 is 1.9125. Each section gets 1.9125 metres.
Check with rounder numbers. 4 sections of nearly 2 metres would be nearly 8 metres, and we had 7.65. That fits.
Careful to take tenths from tenths: 0.6 lines up as 0.60. Then follow the story in order: multiply, subtract, divide.
The bat costs 875.50 rupees. Priya and Arjun have saved some of it, and their grandmother gives the rest, split equally between them. How much does each receive from her?
First, what the two of them have saved. 312.75 plus 248.60 is 561.35.
The bat costs 875.50. How do we find grandmother's gift?

ask.ifNot: They now have exactly enough. So the gift fills the gap between what they saved and what the bat costs. A gap is found by subtracting.

beats.say: 875.50 minus 561.35 is 314.15. That is the whole gift.
Careful: 314.15 is one of the choices, but it is the gift for both children together. Each one gets half.
Half of 314 is 157, and half of 0.15 is 0.075. So each receives 157.075 rupees.
Notice the 3 places after the point. The gift has an odd number of paise, and half of an odd number is never whole. So the exact half needs one more place.
Check: 2 shares of 157.075 make 314.15. And 561.35 plus 314.15 is 875.50, the price of the bat.
So: add what they have, subtract to find the gap, then halve it. And keep every decimal place when you halve.
Ravi buys 3.5 kilograms of rice at 48.60 rupees a kilogram, and 1.75 kilograms of dal at 96.40 a kilogram. He pays with a 500 rupee note. What is his change?

board.text: 3.5 kg at ₹48.60 per kg, 1.75 kg at ₹96.40 per kg

beats.say: Two things to cost, and then the change. Start with the rice. 3.5 kilograms is 3 whole kilograms and a half.
3 times 48.60 is 145.80, and half of 48.60 is 24.30.
145.80 plus 24.30 makes 170.10 rupees for the rice.
Now the dal: 1.75 kilograms. How can we split 1.75 into friendly pieces?

ask.ifNot: 0.75 is three quarters, and three quarters is a half and a quarter. So 1.75 is 1 whole, plus 0.5, plus 0.25.

beats.say: 1 kilogram costs 96.40. Half of that is 48.20. And a quarter is half of the half: 24.10.
Add the three pieces. 96.40 plus 48.20 plus 24.10 is 168.70 rupees for the dal.
Now the whole bill. 170.10 plus 168.70 is 338.80.
We are not finished: the question asks for the change. 500 minus 338.80 is 161.20 rupees.
Check: the bill and the change should make the note again. 338.80 plus 161.20 is 500.
Break each awkward weight into wholes, halves and quarters. Cost the pieces, add for the bill, and take the bill from the note.
On Monday the stall sold 12.5 litres of chai and then 8.75 litres, in cups of 0.25 litres. On Tuesday it took in 1085 rupees at 15.50 a cup. How many more cups were sold on Monday?
We must compare cups with cups. Monday is told in litres and Tuesday in rupees, so we turn each day into cups.
Monday first. 12.5 plus 8.75 is 21.25 litres.
A cup holds 0.25 litres. How many cups are there in 1 litre?

ask.ifNot: 0.25 is a quarter. 4 quarters make a whole, so 1 litre fills 4 cups.

beats.say: So the 21 whole litres fill 84 cups, and the extra quarter litre fills 1 more. Monday: 85 cups.
Tuesday: 15.50 is awkward, so double it. 2 cups cost 31 rupees.
1085 divided by 31 is 35. So that is 35 pairs of cups, which makes 70 cups on Tuesday.
Monday 85 cups, Tuesday 70 cups. 85 minus 70 is 15 more cups on Monday.
Check Tuesday: 70 cups at 15.50 each is 1085 rupees. It works.
Careful: 85 and 70 are both among the choices, but each is only half the story. Turn both days into the same thing, then compare.
Kavya buys 1.25 kilograms of red powder, 0.8 of yellow and 1.45 of blue. She uses 2.75 kilograms for the rangoli. How much is left over?

board.text: Powder: 1.25 kg, 0.8 kg, 1.45 kg. Used 2.75 kg.

beats.say: First we add the three packets. To add 0.8 to the others, how should we write it?

ask.ifNot: 0.8 means 8 tenths. Writing 0.80 keeps the 8 in the tenths place, and gives it 2 places after the point like the others.

beats.say: Now add, with the points in line. 1.25 plus 0.80 is 2.05.
And 2.05 plus 1.45 is 3.50. Kavya has 3.5 kilograms of powder.
She uses 2.75, so we subtract. Count up from 2.75: it takes 0.25 to reach 3, and then 0.50 more to reach 3.50.
0.25 and 0.50 make 0.75. So 0.75 kilograms are left over.
Check: 0.75 left, plus 2.75 used, is 3.50, all the powder.
Careful: the slip here is to put the 8 of 0.8 under the hundredths. Match the decimal points, fill the gaps with zeros, and then add or subtract.
Ravi's laddoos weigh 0.375 kilograms each, and Priya's weigh 0.45 each. A customer buys 4 of Ravi's and some of Priya's, 3.3 kilograms in all. How many of Priya's did he buy?

board.text: Ravi's: 0.375 kg each. Priya's: 0.45 kg each.

beats.say: We know everything about Ravi's laddoos, so start there. 4 times 0.375: double it to get 0.75, and double again to get 1.5 kilograms.
The whole bag weighs 3.3 kilograms. How do we find the weight of Priya's laddoos?

ask.ifNot: The 3.3 kilograms is Ravi's laddoos and Priya's together. Take Ravi's 1.5 away, and what is left must be Priya's.

beats.say: 3.3 minus 1.5 is 1.8 kilograms of Priya's laddoos.
Each of hers weighs 0.45. How many 0.45s make 1.8? Count up: 2 of them weigh 0.9, and 4 of them weigh 1.8.
So the customer bought 4 of Priya's laddoos.
Check the total: Ravi's 1.5 plus Priya's 1.8 is 3.3 kilograms. It works.
Careful not to divide the whole 3.3 by 0.45: part of that weight is Ravi's. Take away the part you know, then divide what is left.
Arjun's family sold 12.5 litres of chai in the morning and 8.75 litres in the evening. Each cup uses 0.25 litres and sells for 15.50 rupees. How much did they earn?

board.text: Sold 12.5 litres and 8.75 litres of chai

beats.say: First, all the chai together. 12.5 plus 8.75 is 21.25 litres.
Each cup takes 0.25 litres. How many cups come out of 1 litre?

ask.ifNot: 0.25 is a quarter, and 4 quarters make 1 whole. So 1 litre fills 4 cups.

beats.say: Every litre makes 4 cups. So the 21 whole litres make 84 cups, and the extra quarter litre makes 1 more. That is 85 cups.
Careful: do not multiply the litres by the price. The 15.50 rupees is for a cup, not for a litre. That is why we needed the number of cups.
Now the money. 85 cups at 15.50 each. 85 times 15 is 1275, and 85 halves are 42.50.
1275 plus 42.50 is 1317.50 rupees.
Check by going back. 1317.50 rupees at 15.50 a cup is 85 cups, and 85 cups of 0.25 litres is 21.25 litres. It fits.
So the chain is: litres, then cups, then rupees. Find how many cups there are before you touch the price.
Rina buys 3 notebooks at 12.65 rupees each, and a story book for 45.50. She pays with a 100 rupee note. How much change does she get?
What does 12.65 rupees pay for?

ask.ifNot: The word each is the clue. 12.65 rupees is for one notebook, and there are 3 of them.

beats.say: So multiply, in two easy parts. 3 times 12 is 36, and 3 times 0.65 is 1.95.
36 plus 1.95 is 37.95 rupees for the notebooks.
Add the story book. 37.95 plus 45.50 is 83.45. That is the whole bill.
Now the change. Careful: take the whole bill from the note, not just one of the prices. 100 minus 83.45 is 16.55 rupees.
Check: the bill and the change together should make the note. 83.45 plus 16.55 is 100.
For a shopping bill: multiply for the things bought in a bunch, add the rest, and take the total from the note.
Riya buys 2.5 kilograms of almonds at 864 rupees a kilogram, and 1.75 kilograms of cashews at 1120 a kilogram. She pays with 5000 rupees. What is her change?

board.text: 2.5 kg at ₹864 per kg, 1.75 kg at ₹1120 per kg

beats.say: Two things to cost, and then the change. Start with the almonds. 2.5 kilograms is 2 whole kilograms and a half.
2 times 864 is 1728, and half of 864 is 432.
1728 plus 432 makes 2160 rupees for the almonds.
Now the cashews: 1.75 kilograms. How can we split 1.75 into friendly pieces?

ask.ifNot: 0.75 is three quarters, and three quarters is a half and a quarter. So 1.75 is 1 whole, plus 0.5, plus 0.25.

beats.say: 1 kilogram costs 1120. Half of that is 560. And a quarter is half of the half: 280.
Add the three pieces. 1120 plus 560 plus 280 is 1960 rupees for the cashews.
Now the whole bill. 2160 plus 1960 is 4120.
We are not finished: the question asks for the change. 5000 minus 4120 is 880 rupees.
Check: the bill and the change should make the note again. 4120 plus 880 is 5000.
Big prices, but the same small idea: wholes, halves and quarters. Cost each piece, add for the bill, then subtract from the money paid.
A customer buys 3 boxes of bangles at 45.75 rupees a box, and a golden bangle for 28.50. The customer pays with a 200 rupee note. How much change must Meera return?
What does 45.75 rupees pay for?

ask.ifNot: The word each is the clue. 45.75 rupees is for one box, and there are 3 of them.

beats.say: So multiply, in two easy parts. 3 times 45 is 135, and 3 times 0.75 is 2.25.
135 plus 2.25 is 137.25 rupees for the boxes.
Add the golden bangle. 137.25 plus 28.50 is 165.75. That is the whole bill.
Now the change. Careful: take the whole bill from the note, not just one of the prices. 200 minus 165.75 is 34.25 rupees.
Check: the bill and the change together should make the note. 165.75 plus 34.25 is 200.
Three steps, in order: multiply for the boxes, add the single thing, subtract the bill from the note.
Aarav buys a geometry box, a pack of pencils and an eraser, and pays with a 100 rupee note. How much change does he get?
What should we work out first?

choices: the price of just one thing
the money he has at the end
ask.ifNot: Several prices went out of the purse. Add them into one total first, and then there is only one subtraction to do.

beats.say: Line up the decimal points and add. 45.60 plus 12.85 is 58.45.
Then 58.45 plus 3.75 is 62.20. That is everything Aarav spent.
Now take that away from the 100 rupee note. Write 100 with a point and two zeros, so the paise have something to be taken from. 100 minus 62.20 leaves 37.80 rupees of change.
Careful: 62.20 is what he spent, not the change. It is one of the choices, waiting to catch you.
Check: the money spent and the change should make the note again. 62.20 plus 37.80 is 100.
So for change: add up the whole bill first, then take it from the note. And keep the decimal points in line.
Ananya's 5 scores are 12.5, 8.75, 15.25, 9.50 and 14.00. She needs 65 in total. How many more does she need?
The plan: add the 5 scores, then see how far the total is from 65.
Look for pairs whose decimal parts fit together. Take 8.75 and 15.25. What do 0.75 and 0.25 make?

ask.ifNot: 0.75 is three quarters, and 0.25 is one quarter. Together they make exactly 1 whole.

beats.say: So 8.75 plus 15.25 is 8 plus 15, plus 1 more. That is 24.
Another pair: 12.5 and 9.50. Each has a half, and the two halves make 1 whole. So that pair comes to 22.
24 plus 22 plus the last score, 14, is 60.
She needs 65. 65 minus 60 is 5 more runs.
Check: 60 plus 5 is 65, the target.
When you add a list of decimals, pair up the ones whose decimal parts make a whole. The sum almost does itself.
Ravi has 200 ladoos. He gives away 0.35 of them, then 0.25 of them, then 0.15 of them, and packs the rest 2.5 to a box. How many boxes does he fill?

board.text: 200 ladoos. Gives away 0.35, 0.25 and 0.15 of them.
The rest are packed 2.5 to a box

beats.say: 0.35 of the ladoos is a part of the whole box, not a number of ladoos. First add the three parts he gives away: 0.35 plus 0.25 plus 0.15 is 0.75.
He gave away 0.75 of the ladoos. What part is left?

ask.ifNot: All the ladoos together are 1 whole. Take away the 0.75 he gave, and 0.25 is left. We do not take 0.75 from 200, because 0.75 is a part, not a number of ladoos.

beats.say: 1 minus 0.75 is 0.25. So a quarter of the ladoos is left.
A quarter of 200 is 50 ladoos.
Each box holds 2.5, so 2 boxes hold 5. And 50 is 10 lots of 5. That is 10 lots of 2 boxes: 20 boxes.
Check: 20 boxes of 2.5 hold 50 ladoos, and 50 is a quarter of 200.
A decimal of something is a part of it. Add the parts, take them from 1 whole, and then find that part of the total.
Ananya starts with 5 litres of lemonade and pours 12 glasses of 0.35 litres each. How much is left in the bottle?
What do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: She pours 12 glasses, not 1. So first find how much lemonade all 12 take, and then take that away from the 5 litres.

beats.say: 12 times 0.35. 10 glasses take 3.5 litres, and 2 glasses take 0.7 litres.
3.5 plus 0.7 is 4.2 litres poured out.
Careful: 4.2 is what went into the glasses, and it is one of the choices. The question asks what is still in the bottle.
5 minus 4.2. From 4.2 up to 5 is 0.8. So 0.8 litres are left.
Check: 4.2 poured, plus 0.8 left, makes 5 litres.
So when the same amount is taken many times, multiply first. Then subtract the total from what you started with.
The friends spent 847.50 rupees on ingredients and took in 1338.75. They give 0.4 of the profit to charity and share the rest among 3. How much does each friend get?

board.text: 0.4 of profit to charity, rest shared by 3

beats.say: Profit is what they took in, minus what they paid out. 1338.75 minus 847.50 is 491.25.
The price of one samosa, 12.75, is just passing by. We already know the total earnings, so we do not need it.
They give 0.4 of the profit to charity. What part of the profit do they keep?

ask.ifNot: The whole profit is 1 whole. Give away 0.4 of it, and 1 minus 0.4 is left. That is 0.6.

beats.say: So they keep 0.6 of 491.25. One tenth of 491.25 is 49.125, and 6 tenths is 6 times that: 294.75.
Now share 294.75 among 3 friends. 294 divided by 3 is 98, and 0.75 divided by 3 is 0.25.
Each friend gets 98.25 rupees.
Check: the charity gets 196.50. Add the 294.75 the friends keep, and we are back at the profit, 491.25.
Careful: sharing the whole profit by 3 forgets the charity. Find the profit, take out the gift, and only then share.
Ravi buys 3.5 kilograms of mangoes at 48.60 rupees a kilogram, and pays with a 200 rupee note. How much change should he get?
First the cost. 3.5 kilograms is 3 whole kilograms and half a kilogram more. So we can split the multiplying into two easy parts.
The 3 whole kilograms: 3 times 48.60 is 145.80.
Now the half kilogram. What does it cost?

choices: half of the price of 1 kilogram
ask.ifNot: 0.5 means one half. So half a kilogram costs half of what a whole kilogram costs.

beats.say: Half of 48.60 is 24.30.
Add the two parts. 145.80 plus 24.30 is 170.10. That is the cost of the mangoes.
Careful: 170.10 is the bill, not the change. Take it from the 200 rupee note. 200 minus 170.10 is 29.90 rupees.
Check: the bill and the change should make the note again. 170.10 plus 29.90 is 200.
So when a weight has a decimal, split it into whole kilograms and the bit left over. Cost each part, add, and then find the change.
Rohit bats for 2 sessions. We know the overs and the runs per over in each. How many runs does he score altogether?
Runs per over, times the number of overs, gives the runs. So each session is one multiplication, and then we add the two.
First session: 12.5 times 6.4. Split 12.5 into 10 and 2.5. 10 times 6.4 is 64.
And 2.5 times 6.4? Here is a hint: 2.5 is a quarter of 10.

ask.ifNot: 10 times 6.4 was 64. And 2.5 is a quarter of 10, so we want a quarter of 64. 4 times 16 is 64, so a quarter of 64 is 16.

beats.say: 64 plus 16 is 80 runs in the first session.
Second session: 7.5 times 8.2. 7 times 8.2 is 57.4, and half of 8.2 is 4.1.
57.4 plus 4.1 is 61.5 runs in the second session.
Altogether: 80 plus 61.5 is 141.5 runs.
Check the second session another way. 7.5 times 8 is 60, and 7.5 times 0.2 is 1.5. That makes 61.5 again.
Careful not to drop the 0.5 at the end of 61.5: one of the choices is waiting for that slip. Split an awkward decimal into easy pieces, multiply each, and add.
Sneha has 15.6 kilograms of besan. She uses 2.35 kilograms a day for 4 days, and on day 5 she uses all that is left. How much is that?

board.text: 15.6 kg of besan. Uses 2.35 kg a day for 4 days.

beats.say: What do we need before we can find day 5?

ask.ifNot: She uses 2.35 kilograms on each of 4 days, not just once. And day 5 is not an equal share: it is whatever is left. So first find what the 4 days used.

beats.say: 4 times 2.35. Double it: 4.70. Double again: 9.40. So 9.40 kilograms are gone after 4 days.
Now subtract from 15.6. Write it as 15.60, so the decimal points line up.
15.60 minus 9.40 is 6.20. On day 5 she uses 6.20 kilograms.
Check: 9.40 used in 4 days, plus 6.20 on day 5, is 15.60. That is all the besan.
Notice that day 5 uses far more than the other days. That is fine: the story says she uses whatever is left.
So multiply for the equal days, then subtract from the start. And write in a zero when one number has fewer decimal places.
Ravi buys 2.5 kilograms of mangoes. Each kilogram costs 84.60 rupees, and he pays with a 500 rupee note. What change does he receive?
We need the cost before the change. Think of 2.5 kilograms as 2 whole kilograms, and then half a kilogram. Two easy parts.
The 2 whole kilograms: 2 times 84.60 is 169.20.
Now the half kilogram. What does it cost?

choices: half of the price of 1 kilogram
ask.ifNot: 0.5 means one half. So half a kilogram costs half of what a whole kilogram costs.

beats.say: Half of 84.60 is 42.30.
Add the two parts. 169.20 plus 42.30 is 211.50. That is the cost of the mangoes.
Careful: 211.50 is the bill, not the change. Take it from the 500 rupee note. 500 minus 211.50 is 288.50 rupees.
Check: the bill and the change should make the note again. 211.50 plus 288.50 is 500.
A decimal weight is just whole kilograms plus a part of one. Multiply each piece by the price, add them, and subtract from the note.
Ananya buys 3.75 kilograms of kaju katli and 2.5 kilograms of gulab jamun. The shopkeeper takes off 0.50 rupees for every 100 grams she buys. What does she pay?

board.text: 3.75 kg at ₹480 per kg, 2.5 kg at ₹260 per kg

beats.say: First the price with no discount. Kaju katli: 3.75 is 3 and three quarters. 3 times 480 is 1440, and three quarters of 480 is 360.
1440 plus 360 is 1800 rupees.
Gulab jamun: 2 times 260 is 520, and half of 260 is 130. That makes 650 rupees.
Before the discount, the bill is 1800 plus 650, which is 2450 rupees.
Now the discount. It depends on the weight, so add the weights: 3.75 plus 2.5 is 6.25 kilograms of sweets.
The discount is 0.50 rupees for every 100 grams. How many lots of 100 grams are there in 1 kilogram?

ask.ifNot: 1 kilogram is 1000 grams, and 1000 is 10 hundreds. So each kilogram holds 10 lots of 100 grams.

beats.say: 10 lots of 0.50 is 5. So the discount is 5 rupees for every kilogram.
6.25 kilograms, with 5 rupees off each: 6.25 times 5 is 31.25 rupees off.
2450 minus 31.25 is 2418.75 rupees. That is what Ananya pays.
Check the discount another way. 6.25 kilograms is 62.5 lots of 100 grams, and 62.5 times 0.50 is 31.25 again.
Careful: the discount is not 0.50 just once. It is 0.50 for every 100 grams, so it grows with the weight. Price first, discount second, then subtract.
Mangoes cost 64.50 rupees a kilogram. Ravi buys 3.5 kilograms and pays with a 500 rupee note. How much change does he receive?
Cost first, change second. 3.5 kilograms means 3 whole kilograms and one half kilogram. Let's cost the two parts one at a time.
The 3 whole kilograms: 3 times 64.50 is 193.50.
Now the half kilogram. What does it cost?

choices: half of the price of 1 kilogram
ask.ifNot: 0.5 means one half. So half a kilogram costs half of what a whole kilogram costs.

beats.say: Half of 64.50 is 32.25.
Add the two parts. 193.50 plus 32.25 is 225.75. That is the cost of the mangoes.
Careful: 225.75 is the bill, not the change. Take it from the 500 rupee note. 500 minus 225.75 is 274.25 rupees.
Check: the bill and the change should make the note again. 225.75 plus 274.25 is 500.
Remember the two stops on the way: the whole kilograms, then the half. Only after both are added do we subtract from the note.
Riya has 500 rupees. She buys 3 boxes of sparklers and 2 packets of rangoli powder, then shares what is left equally among 4 friends. How much does each friend get?

board.text: The rest is shared equally by 4 friends

beats.say: Sparklers: 3 times 48 is 144, and 3 times 0.75 is 2.25. So 146.25 rupees.
Rangoli powder: 2 times 62.50 is 125 rupees.
Spent altogether: 146.25 plus 125 is 271.25. So what is left is 500 minus 271.25, which is 228.75.
228.75 rupees for 4 friends. What is a quick way to divide by 4?

ask.ifNot: Sharing among 4 is the same as cutting in half, and then cutting each half in half. 2 times 2 is 4.

beats.say: Half of 228.75 is 114.375. And half of that is 57.1875.
Money stops at paise, 2 places after the point. So we round 57.1875. The digit after the 8 is a 7, so the 8 rounds up to 9.
Each friend gets about 57.19 rupees.
Check: 4 times 57.19 is 228.76. That is just 1 paisa more than 228.75, and that tiny gap is the rounding.
So: find what is left, share it, and when the answer is money, round it to 2 places at the very end.
Priya buys 3 packets of diyas and a rangoli colour set. She gets a discount, and hands over a 200 rupee note. How much more does she still have to pay?
Diyas: 3 times 45 is 135, and 3 times 0.75 is 2.25. That is 137.25 rupees.
Add the colour set. 137.25 plus 128.60 is 265.85.
The shopkeeper gives a discount of 12.35. What does a discount do to the bill?

ask.ifNot: A discount is money taken off the price, a little gift from the shopkeeper. So the bill goes down, and we subtract.

beats.say: 265.85 minus 12.35 is 253.50. That is the final bill.
Now look closely. The bill is 253.50, but Priya handed over only 200. This time there is no change: she still owes money.
253.50 minus 200 is 53.50 rupees more to pay.
Check: the 200 she paid, plus 53.50 more, is 253.50, the final bill.
Careful: we usually take the bill from the note. Here the bill is bigger, so we take the note from the bill. Always look at which number is larger.
Ravi buys 2.5 kilograms of apples at 120.50 rupees a kilogram, and 1.75 kilograms of oranges at 80.40 a kilogram. He pays with a 500 rupee note. What is his change?

board.text: 2.5 kg at ₹120.50 per kg, 1.75 kg at ₹80.40 per kg

beats.say: Two things to cost, and then the change. Start with the apples. 2.5 kilograms is 2 whole kilograms and a half.
2 times 120.50 is 241, and half of 120.50 is 60.25.
241 plus 60.25 makes 301.25 rupees for the apples.
Now the oranges: 1.75 kilograms. How can we split 1.75 into friendly pieces?

ask.ifNot: 0.75 is three quarters, and three quarters is a half and a quarter. So 1.75 is 1 whole, plus 0.5, plus 0.25.

beats.say: 1 kilogram costs 80.40. Half of that is 40.20. And a quarter is half of the half: 20.10.
Add the three pieces. 80.40 plus 40.20 plus 20.10 is 140.70 rupees for the oranges.
Now the whole bill. 301.25 plus 140.70 is 441.95.
We are not finished: the question asks for the change. 500 minus 441.95 is 58.05 rupees.
Check: the bill and the change should make the note again. 441.95 plus 58.05 is 500.
Halves and quarters turn a hard multiplication into a few easy ones. Keep each piece on the board, add them up, and then find the change.
Priya buys 4 packets of sparklers at 12.75 rupees each, and a box of diyas for 8.50. How much does she spend altogether?
What does 12.75 rupees pay for?

ask.ifNot: The word each is the clue. 12.75 is the price of one packet, and Priya buys 4 of them.

beats.say: So multiply, in two easy parts. 4 times 12 is 48, and 4 times 0.75 is 3.
48 plus 3 is 51 rupees for the sparklers.
Careful: 51 is one of the choices, but the diyas are not in it yet.
51 plus 8.50 is 59.50 rupees in all.
Check with round numbers. 4 packets at about 13 rupees is 52, and about 8 more makes 60. Our 59.50 is right beside it.
So when a story says each, multiply first. Then add on everything else that was bought.
Ananya's mother buys 5.75 litres of milk in the morning and 3.25 litres in the evening. Each cup of chai needs 0.125 litres of milk and sells for 12.50 rupees. How much does she earn?

board.text: Each cup: 0.125 litres of milk, sold for ₹12.50

beats.say: First, all the milk together. 5.75 plus 3.25 is 9 litres.
Each cup takes 0.125 litres. How many cups come out of 1 litre?

ask.ifNot: 0.125 is one eighth. Count up in steps of 0.125, and the 8th step lands exactly on 1. So 1 litre makes 8 cups.

beats.say: Every litre makes 8 cups. So 9 litres make 9 times 8, which is 72 cups.
Careful: do not multiply the litres by the price. The 12.50 rupees is for a cup, not for a litre. That is why we needed the number of cups.
Now the money. 72 cups at 12.50 each. 72 times 12 is 864, and 72 halves are 36.
864 plus 36 is 900 rupees.
Check by going back. 900 rupees at 12.50 a cup is 72 cups, and 72 cups of 0.125 litres is 9 litres. It fits.
Milk, then cups, then money. Each step needs the one before it, so take them in order.
Ravi sells 3 sizes of chai on match day, and he has to buy milk, tea leaves and sugar. What is his profit for the day?
Before we start, sort the numbers. 150, 250 and 400 millilitres are cup sizes. They are not money, so we set them aside.
What is profit?

ask.ifNot: Profit is what you really gain. Count the money that came in, then take away what had to be paid out.

beats.say: Start with the money earned. Small cups: 24 at 12.50 each. 24 times 12 is 288, and 24 halves are 12 more. That is 300 rupees.
Medium cups: 36 times 18 is 648, and 36 times 0.75 is 27. Together, 675 rupees.
Large cups: 15 times 28 is 420 rupees.
Add the three: 300 plus 675 plus 420 is 1395 rupees earned.
Now the spending: 485.60 on milk, 124.40 on tea leaves and 90 on sugar. Together that is 700.
Profit is earned minus spent. 1395 minus 700 is 695 rupees.
Check: profit plus spending should give back the earnings. 695 plus 700 is 1395.
Careful: the money earned is one of the choices, but that is not profit yet. Earned, minus spent: that is profit.
Three shops sell fairy lights, each with its own kind of price. We need exactly 25 metres. Which shop is cheapest, and what do we pay there?

board.text: Shop C: 10 m for ₹140, then ₹15.50 a metre

beats.say: The prices are told in three different ways, so we cannot compare them yet. We work out what 25 metres costs at each shop.
Shop A: 25 times 12.75. 25 times 12 is 300, and 25 times 0.75 is 18.75. So 318.75 rupees.
Shop B charges 1350 rupees for 100 metres. What is a quick way to get the price of 25 metres?

ask.ifNot: 25 metres is a quarter of 100 metres. So it costs a quarter of the price of 100 metres.

beats.say: Half of 1350 is 675, and half of 675 is 337.50. So Shop B costs 337.50 rupees.
Shop C: the first 10 metres cost 140 rupees. That leaves 15 metres to buy at 15.50 each.
15 times 15 is 225, and 15 halves are 7.50 more. That is 232.50 for the extra metres.
With the 140 for the first 10 metres, Shop C costs 372.50 rupees.
Now we can compare: 318.75, 337.50 and 372.50. The smallest is Shop A, at 318.75 rupees.
Check A against B another way. 100 metres at Shop A would cost 1275 rupees, which is less than Shop B's 1350. So A really does beat B.
Careful with Shop C: its 15.50 price is only for the metres after the first 10. When prices come in different forms, turn each into the cost of exactly what you need.
Poonam has 16.75 rupees, Urmila has 25.25 and Anjali has 9.05. How much do they have in all?
With money, the part before the point is rupees, and the part after it is paise. A tidy way is to add the rupees and the paise separately.
Rupees first: 16 plus 25 plus 9 is 50.
Now the paise: 75 plus 25 plus 5 is 105.
105 paise. How do we write that in rupees?

ask.ifNot: 100 paise make 1 rupee. So 105 paise is 1 rupee and 5 paise more, and we write that as 1.05.

beats.say: So the total is 50 rupees plus 1.05 rupees. That is 51.05.
Careful with 9.05. It is 9 rupees and 5 paise, not 50 paise. The zero after the point holds the place.
Check by adding with the points in line. 16.75 plus 25.25 is 42, and 42 plus 9.05 is 51.05.
So add rupees to rupees and paise to paise. When the paise pass 100, they hand 1 rupee over.
Asha has 16.25 rupees, Reeta has 60.05 and Geeta has 33.75. How much do they have in all?
Write the three amounts one under another, with the decimal points in line. Then add from the right, just as with whole numbers.
Hundredths: 5 plus 5 plus 5 is 15. Write the 5 and carry 1.
Tenths: 2 plus 0 plus 7 is 9, and the carried 1 makes 10. Write 0 and carry 1.
Ones: 6 plus 0 plus 3 is 9, and the carried 1 makes 10 again. Write 0 and carry 1.
Tens column: 1 plus 6 plus 3, and the carried 1. What goes there?

ask.ifNot: 1 plus 6 plus 3 is 10, and the carry makes it 11. Leave out that carry and you get 10, which is exactly the trap in this question.

beats.say: So the total is 110.05 rupees.
Now look at the choices: 100, 100.05 and 100.75. Ours is 110.05, and it is not there. So the answer is None of these.
Check with rupees and paise apart. 16 plus 60 plus 33 is 109 rupees. The paise make 105, which is 1 rupee more and 5 paise. 110.05 again.
Careful: 100.05 looks so close that it is tempting. Trust your working. If you carried properly and your total is not listed, None of these is right.
Rohan's coins split into groups of 5 with none left over, and into groups of 3 with none left over. And he has between 40 and 60 coins.

board.text: Groups of 5: none left. Groups of 3: none left.

beats.say: None left over in 5s means the number is a multiple of 5. None left over in 3s means it is a multiple of 3 as well.
A number that is a multiple of both 3 and 5 must be a multiple of what?

ask.ifNot: Count in 5s until you land on a multiple of 3: 5, 10, 15. So 15 is the first number they share, and every other shared one is a multiple of 15.

beats.say: 3 times 5 is 15. So let's count in 15s: 15, 30, 45, 60.
Which of these lies between 40 and 60? Only 45. And 60 itself is the edge, so it is not between.
Rohan has 45 coins.
Check both clues. 45 divided by 5 is 9, and 45 divided by 3 is 15. Nothing left over either time.
Careful: plenty of numbers here split into 5s but leave coins over in 3s. For two clues at once, find the first number both share, then count in that.
Riya has 84 chocolates, 126 toffees and 42 diyas. Every bag must get the same of each, with nothing left over. What is the greatest number of bags?
Each pile is shared out equally among the bags. So the number of bags must divide 84, and 126, and 42 exactly.
We want the greatest number of bags. So what are we looking for?

choices: the biggest number that divides all 3
the smallest number all 3 go into
ask.ifNot: The bags share each pile out, so the number of bags has to divide each pile. The most bags means the greatest number that divides all 3.

beats.say: Here is a shortcut. There cannot be more than 42 bags, because there are only 42 diyas. So let's test 42 itself.
Does 42 divide 84? Yes, 2 times. Does it divide 126? Yes, 3 times. And it divides itself once.
So 42 divides all 3 piles, and nothing bigger could. The greatest number of bags is 42.
We can check with prime factors too. 84 is 2 times 2 times 3 times 7. 126 is 2 times 3 times 3 times 7. And 42 is 2 times 3 times 7.
What all 3 share is one 2, one 3 and one 7. And 2 times 3 times 7 is 42. It agrees.
Careful: a smaller number like 7 divides all 3 piles too. But the question wants the greatest, so always test the biggest number that could work.
Each bag gets 2 chocolates, 3 toffees and 1 diya. Sharing several piles into the most equal groups means finding their greatest common factor.
Three clues about Rohan's coins. In 2s, 1 is left over. In 3s, 1 is left over. In 5s, none is left over. And there are fewer than 50.
Which clue is the easiest one to start with?

ask.ifNot: A clue with nothing left over gives a simple list: the multiples of 5. The other clues can then cross numbers off that list.

beats.say: So write the multiples of 5 below 50.
Next clue: in 2s, 1 is left over. That means the number is odd. So cross out the even ones.
5 numbers are still standing: 5, 15, 25, 35 and 45. Last clue: in 3s, there must be 1 left over.
15 and 45 are in the 3 times table, so they leave nothing over. 5 leaves 2 over, and so does 35.
That leaves 25. It is 8 threes, and 1 more. So 1 is left over, just as the clue says.
Rohan has 25 coins.
Check all three clues. 25 is 12 twos and 1 more, 8 threes and 1 more, and exactly 5 fives.
With several clues, start with the simplest one to make a list. Then let each of the other clues cross numbers off.
N is divisible by both 4 and 9, it lies between 300 and 400, and it is as large as it can be. We want the sum of its digits.

board.text: N divisible by 4 and 9, between 300 and 400
N as large as possible. Sum of digits = ?

beats.say: 4 and 9 share no factors. So a number that both of them divide must be a multiple of 4 times 9, which is 36.
So we are hunting for the largest multiple of 36 below 400. Start from an easy one: 36 times 10 is 360.
360 is in the range. Can we fit one more 36 in before 400?

ask.ifNot: Add 36 to 360 and you get 396, which is still below 400. Add another 36 and you jump past 400. So 396 is the largest.

beats.say: 36 times 11 is 396. The next one, 432, is too big. So N is 396.
Careful, we are not finished. The question asks for the sum of the digits of N, not for N itself.
3 plus 9 plus 6 is 18.
Check N. 396 divided by 4 is 99, and 396 divided by 9 is 44. Both are exact.
So: join the two divisors into one, find the largest multiple in the range, and then answer what was really asked.
Riya has 2023 diyas. She tries rows of 7, rows of 11 and rows of 17. How many of those row sizes leave no diyas over?
A row size works only if it divides 2023 exactly. So we test each one. Start with 7, and here is a neat way: 2023 is 2100 minus 77.
7 goes into 2100 exactly 300 times, and into 77 exactly 11 times. So 7 goes into 2023 exactly: 300 minus 11, which is 289 times.
Now 11. There is a quick test: take the digits in turn, subtracting and adding. For 2023 that is 2 minus 0 plus 2 minus 3. What do we get?

ask.ifNot: Go one digit at a time. 2 minus 0 is 2, plus 2 is 4, minus 3 is 1.

beats.say: 11 divides a number only when that test gives 0 or a multiple of 11. We got 1, so 11 does not work. Rows of 11 would leave 10 diyas over.
Last, 17. We found that 2023 is 7 times 289. And 289 is 17 times 17. So 17 goes in exactly too: 119 times.
Careful: the question does not ask which row sizes work. It asks how many of them work.
7 works, 11 does not, and 17 works. That is 2 of the 3 row sizes.
Check by multiplying back: 7 times 17 times 17 is 2023.
To test a divisor, divide, or use a quick rule if you know one. Then read the question again to see what it really wants.
Arjun has 180 players to put into equal teams, with nobody left out. Each team must have more than 10 but fewer than 25 players. How many team sizes are possible?

board.text: Team size: more than 10, fewer than 25

beats.say: Equal teams with nobody left out means the team size divides 180 exactly. It must be a factor of 180.
Factors come in pairs that multiply to 180. Start from 1 and work up: 1 times 180, 2 times 90, 3 times 60, and on, until the pairs meet at 12 times 15.
The team size must be more than 10 and fewer than 25. Does 10 itself count?

ask.ifNot: More than 10 means bigger than 10. So 10 itself is left out, and so is 25 at the other end.

beats.say: Now pick out the factors that lie between 10 and 25. They are 12, 15, 18 and 20.
The next factor up is 30, which is too big. And 9 and 10 are too small.
So there are 4 possible team sizes.
Check a couple. Teams of 18 make 10 teams, because 10 times 18 is 180. And teams of 15 make 12 teams.
Careful: the answer is how many sizes there are, not one of the sizes. List the factor pairs in order so that none is missed, then count the ones in range.
Riya lists the factors of 720 that are prime numbers, and adds them up. What total does she get?
To find the prime factors, we break 720 down until only prime numbers are left. 720 is 72 times 10. That is a friendly start.
10 is 2 times 5. And 72 is 8 times 9.
8 is 2 times 2 times 2, and 9 is 3 times 3. Now every piece is prime.
Riya writes each prime factor once in her list. Which list is hers?

ask.ifNot: A list of factors names each number once, however many times it is used. And 1 is not a prime number. So her list is 2, 3 and 5.

beats.say: 2 plus 3 plus 5 is 10.
Check that each one really divides 720. It is even, so 2 works. It ends in 0, so 5 works. And its digits add to 9, so 3 works.
Careful not to add every 2 and every 3 in the long line. Break the number into primes, then count each prime once.
Arjun's samosas go into groups of 2, or 3, or 5, with none left over each time. He has more than 50 but fewer than 80.

board.text: Groups of 2, 3 or 5: none left over

beats.say: Nothing left over in 2s, 3s or 5s. So the number is a multiple of 2, and of 3, and of 5, all at the same time.
What is the smallest number that 2, 3 and 5 all divide?

ask.ifNot: 10 splits into 2s and 5s, but not into 3s. 15 splits into 3s and 5s, but not into 2s. We need all three at once, and that first happens at 30.

beats.say: 2 times 3 times 5 is 30. Every number that works is a multiple of 30.
Which one is more than 50 and fewer than 80? 30 is too small and 90 is too big. Only 60 fits.
Check. 60 divided by 2 is 30. 60 divided by 3 is 20. 60 divided by 5 is 12. No remainders.
Careful with the other choices. 70 will not split into 3s, 75 will not split into 2s, and 72 will not split into 5s. Each one passes two tests but not all three.
So when a number must split into several group sizes, find the smallest number they all share, then count in that.
Riya shares 84 chocolates equally among her friends, with none left over. One of these numbers of friends is impossible. Which?

board.text: 84 chocolates shared equally, none left over

beats.say: Equal shares with none left over means the number of friends divides 84 exactly. We are hunting for the one that does not. So we test each choice.
84 divided by 6 is 14. Exact, so 6 friends is possible. And the same fact tells us 14 works too: 84 divided by 14 is 6.
84 divided by 12 is 7. Exact again.
Now 16. If each of 16 friends takes 5 chocolates, that uses 80. What happens to the last 4 chocolates?

ask.ifNot: Each friend has 5, and that uses 80 of the 84. Only 4 remain, far too few to give another one to all 16 friends. So they are left over.

beats.say: 84 is 16 times 5, with 4 left over. So 16 does not divide 84.
The number of friends cannot be 16.
A quick check: 84 is 4 times 21. Now 16 is 4 times 4, and 4 does not go into 21. So 16 cannot go into 84.
Careful with the word cannot: we wanted the one that does not fit. Test each choice by dividing, and look for a remainder.
